title: Judicial integrity: Controlled assistance replaces blanket bans
desc: Balances concrete harms and prospective benefits through human engagement, lifecycle governance, privacy and staff supervision.

kps.k: Courts are converging on controlled, assistive AI use rather than blanket prohibition or autonomous adjudication.
kps.d: The substantive proposition is that AI may support judicial administration, legal research, drafting and court-document preparation, but human judicial authority and responsibility must remain intact. England and Wales treats generative AI as a potentially useful secondary tool; Victoria conditionally permits court users to employ AI in preparing documents; Canada permits support systems but categorically rejects delegating judicial decisions to any person or computer program. Hong Kong similarly subordinates efficiency to judicial independence, impartiality, accountability and public confidence. This is principally a normative institutional position, not an empirically demonstrated balance of benefits and risks.

qs.q: AI tools may assist, but they cannot replace direct judicial engagement with evidence.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (refreshed 31 October 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: 1.5 Court users can utilise AI in the preparation of Court documents if they comply with this Practice Note.
qs.a: Practice Note SC Gen 25 — The Use of Artificial Intelligence by Court Users · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Judicial integrity, rights and public confidence provide the governing standard.
kps.d: The guidance frames responsible AI use around the administration of justice rather than productivity alone. Recurring objectives include judicial independence, fairness, impartiality, accountability, transparency, accessibility, the rule of law and human rights. UNESCO-oriented guidance assigns courts an active role in shaping AI before, during and after deployment, while national guidance applies these principles to procurement, configuration and daily use. The practical implication is that courts should assess AI as an institutional governance issue, not leave adoption solely to individual judges or technology teams.

qs.q: Any use of AI by or on behalf of the judiciary must be consistent with the judiciary’s overarching obligation to protect the integrity of the administration of justice.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (refreshed 31 October 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Courts have the power to control and shape how AI systems are developed and used to safeguard judicial independence, the rule of law, and human rights.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of AI Systems in Courts and Tribunals · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Human responsibility, direct engagement and verification are the main safeguards, but their limits remain contested.
kps.d: England and Wales requires judges to read underlying documents and remain personally responsible for material produced in their names; it also preserves legal representatives’ responsibility for accurate and appropriate submissions. Canadian guidance adds verification to the trust framework and recommends caution proportionate to AI’s uncertain impact. It nevertheless acknowledges a central qualification: human verification may become unachievable for some evolving systems, and checking legality—including privacy and copyright—goes beyond checking factual content. The sources therefore agree on human accountability but do not resolve when an AI system becomes too opaque or complex for meaningful oversight. England and Wales also says judges generally need not disclose preparatory work behind judgments, creating a qualified transparency boundary rather than a universal AI-disclosure rule.

qs.q: Take Responsibility  Judicial office holders are personally responsible for material which is produced in their name.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (refreshed 31 October 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: All legal representatives are responsible for the material they put before the court/tribunal and have a professional obligation to ensure it is accurate and appropriate.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI): Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (31 October 2025 refresh) · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Concrete harms support caution, while claimed benefits remain mostly prospective or unquantified.
kps.d: The strongest concrete evidence in the material concerns misuse: two reported UK High Court matters involved AI-generated arguments citing nonexistent cases, with wasted costs, delays and a fine. Broader guidance identifies bias, discrimination, errors, hallucinations, confidentiality failures and security risks. By contrast, claims that AI can enhance access to justice, productivity, human rights or justice delivery are generally framed as potential benefits. A white paper reports operational deployment of secure chat tools and semantic search and asserts time-saving and decision-support gains, but the supplied extracts provide no quantitative evaluation. References to legal-AI reliability studies do not reproduce their methods or findings and therefore cannot establish error rates here.

qs.q: In two separate cases, lawyers submitted AI-generated legal arguments containing citations to non-existent cases.
qs.a: Global Judges' Initiative: Survey on the Use of AI Systems by Judicial Operators · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Yet, how can we ensure that the benefits of AI outweigh its risks (bias, discrimination, errors and hallucinations)?
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of AI Systems in Courts and Tribunals · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Operational governance extends beyond output accuracy to security, privacy, training data, staff supervision and scope.
kps.d: The guidance recommends secure tools and work devices, approval processes, breach procedures and supervision of clerks and other staff. Canadian guidance stresses that even accurate output may create privacy, intellectual-property or consent problems because models may use sensitive court or litigant data. Policies also define coverage broadly: New York applies its interim rules to judges and nonjudicial employees and to court work on any device; Singapore and Victoria address court users beyond lawyers, including self-represented persons and witnesses. Courts therefore need controls covering devices, data inputs, vendor and model selection, staff conduct and non-lawyer users—not merely proofreading final text.

qs.q: Use work devices (rather than personal devices) to access AI tools.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (refreshed 31 October 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: GUIDELINE 3: HAVE REGARD TO THE LEGAL ASPECTS OF AI USE  Court administrators and Chief Justices must ensure that the integration of AI into any court process must consistently adhere to applicable laws, including those governing privacy, intellectual property, and criminal activities.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Canadian Courts (Canadian Judicial Council, First Edition, September 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Governance must remain adaptive and locally tailored because technologies, uses and impacts differ.
kps.d: The material covers generative AI alongside established applications such as technology-assisted review, semantic search and routine predictive systems; it cautions against treating their risk profiles as interchangeable. Jurisdictions also divide audiences differently, issuing separate or combined guidance for judges, staff, lawyers, litigants and other participants. New York labels its policy interim, Canada expects continuous revision, and UNESCO-oriented guidance favours frameworks suited to local conditions. Practical implementation therefore requires periodic impact monitoring, education and policy revision rather than a fixed one-time rulebook. Important limitations remain: several supplied excerpts contain only definitions, opening provisions, references or links, so they do not establish the full restrictions or safeguards adopted in those instruments.

qs.q: For example, TAR is now part of the landscape of approaches to electronic disclosure.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (refreshed 31 October 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: This interim policy is intended to evolve with technological advancements, operational necessities, and future iterations of relevant legislation, regulation, and public policy.
qs.a: Interim Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (New York State Unified Court System) · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The curated regulators, courts and professional-body sources substantively support the proposition that judicial AI should be permitted as controlled assistance, not used for autonomous adjudication or prohibited outright. Their common rationale is institutional rather than primarily productivity-based: AI use must preserve judicial authority, direct engagement with evidence, accountability, fairness, security, privacy and public confidence. The clearest guidance conditionally permits AI for secondary tasks or court-document preparation while keeping responsibility with judges and court users. Material variation concerns emphasis and operational depth. England and Wales foregrounds direct engagement, personal responsibility, secure devices and staff supervision; Canada most clearly prohibits delegation of judicial decisions and extends governance to procurement, verification, training data, privacy and continuing monitoring; Hong Kong stresses judicial integrity; New York and UNESCO-oriented guidance emphasise adaptive, lifecycle and locally tailored governance. A UK white paper builds on the proposition with reported implementation of secure assistive tools, although its benefit claims are unquantified. Other supplied fragments merely provide definitions, provenance or links, so their individual positions remain unclear. Across this curated selection, no substantive source rejects the principal proposition, but the sources do not resolve when verification becomes inadequate or provide strong empirical evidence that claimed benefits outweigh risks.

qs.q: It must be unequivocally understood that no judge is permitted to delegate decision-making authority, whether to a law clerk, administrative assistant, or computer program, regardless of their capabilities.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Canadian Courts (Canadian Judicial Council, First Edition, September 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The substantive 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that courts should permit controlled, assistive AI use while retaining human judicial authority and governing adoption through judicial-integrity safeguards. The common rationale is that efficiency or administrative assistance cannot override independence, impartiality, accountability, rights, fairness or public confidence. The Canadian guidance most clearly distinguishes permissible support from impermissible delegation and extends governance across procurement, deployment, configuration, legal compliance, verification, monitoring and education. Hong Kong similarly allows AI to support judicial and administrative work, but subjects use to advance risk assessment and the integrity of justice administration. The Global Judges’ Initiative reinforces the case for caution by reporting fabricated-citation incidents and describing AI’s effects as uneven and unpredictable, although it provides less operational detail. Material internal variation concerns scope and evidential completeness: Canada acknowledges that meaningful human verification may not always be achievable and highlights privacy, copyright and training-data risks beyond output accuracy; Hong Kong focuses more tightly on institutional principles and risk assessment. The supplied Victoria and Singapore fragments establish provenance, coverage and definitions but contain too little substantive guidance to determine their positions. Accordingly, they do not contradict the broader support visible in the substantive sources. Because this is a curated selection, the alignment should not be treated as evidence of prevalence across courts generally.

qs.q: It must be unequivocally understood that no judge is permitted to delegate decision-making authority, whether to a law clerk, administrative assistant, or computer program, regardless of their capabilities.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Canadian Courts (Canadian Judicial Council, First Edition, September 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Specifically, technology serves to support the Judiciary in performing its role and functions more effectively and efficiently, without compromising the principles of judicial independence, impartiality, and accountability.
qs.a: Guidelines on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence for Judges and Judicial Officers and Support Staff of the Hong Kong Judiciary · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources accept the proposition that courts should permit assistive AI under human authority rather than impose blanket bans or allow autonomous adjudication. Collectively, they materially develop it from a general principle into an institutional adoption model: judiciary-wide policies, secure deployment, device and workforce coverage, staff supervision, training, accountability, privacy, accuracy and revision as technology changes. The clearest implementation evidence is the reported UK deployment of secure tools for drafting, summarising, analysis and case-information retrieval, while New York extends governance across judges, nonjudicial employees and court work on any device. Common reasons are protection of judicial integrity, fairness, security and public confidence while retaining potential productivity benefits. Material variation concerns specificity and evidential strength: the England and Wales guidance is explicit that AI is only a secondary tool and cannot replace direct engagement with evidence; lifecycle guidance emphasises court-led, locally tailored governance; the white paper reports adoption and asserts operational gains but supplies no quantitative evaluation; and two NSW records merely link to other guidance, leaving their substantive position unclear. The two England and Wales records substantially duplicate the same refreshed guidance and should not be treated as independent evidence. Overall, these sources show governance and implementation advancing together, but they do not demonstrate at scale that claimed benefits outweigh risks.

qs.q: AI tools may assist, but they cannot replace direct judicial engagement with evidence.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (refreshed 31 October 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The 2026 source supports the proposition that courts should permit controlled, assistive AI use rather than impose a blanket ban. The Supreme Court of Victoria conditionally allows court users to use AI when preparing court documents, while explicitly pairing potential access-to-justice benefits with awareness of limitations and risks. This is institutional guidance for all court users, not evidence that the anticipated benefits have been realised. Because only one source is supplied for this period, there is no meaningful cross-source variation to assess. Material limits remain within the source itself: the excerpt does not specify the required safeguards, address verification or lifecycle governance in detail, or state a position on autonomous adjudication.
